title: Denmark to ban mink farming in government U-turn
summary:
Mink farming will end in Denmark by August 2029 after the government decided to drop plans to pursue an exemption to an EU-wide ban on the practice.
Denmark was once the largest producer of mink fur in the world, but the industry has declined due to global bans on fur farming, a decline in the fur trade and an earlier outbreak of a Covid strain in the nation's mink population.
"It is absolutely the right decision not to apply for a special scheme for mink breeding in Denmark," she said.
The Danish Mink Association, which represents breeders, has been approached for comment.
Denmark is one of the few European countries to still produce mink fur, one of the more common pelts used in making fur garments.

title: Clean Energy Has a Lot Riding on the AI Data Center Boom
summary:
But a slowing data center build out leaves less mature technologies at risk.
From advanced geothermal to new ways of producing nuclear power, big tech companies have been willing to pay more to lock in reliable power sources, thereby accelerating the market for these new efforts.
Even unproven technologies like nuclear fusion have received a big financial boost from tech firms speculating that they might help solve their power challenges and give them a competitive leg up in the AI race.
In a tighter financial environment with lower projected electricity demand, both the incentive and the financial capacity to make bold bets diminish.

title: Denmark nurdles may be from River Tyne spill, says Danish environment agency
summary:
Nurdles found along the Danish coast are likely to originate from the spill in north-east England, according to the country's environment agency.
Masses of plastic pellets were found along the western coast of Denmark in September.
The Danish Environment Protection Agency has now confirmed tests carried out on the microplastics suggest they originated from the River Tyne spill in July.
Signe Simonsen, the head of startup Race for Oceans Technology, first spotted the nurdles on the island of Mandø in Denmark on 26 September.
"There were just so many milk white plastic pellets," she said.

title: For Black voters, climate action means little without relief from rising costs
summary:
Black voters may not name climate change as their biggest election concern, but they still want leaders to address it.
At the same time, most respondents said they wanted climate policy to be a top issue for their elected officials.
Erica Tebbs, a senior analyst at HIT Strategies, said the problem is not convincing Black voters that environmental threats exist.
The poll found substantial concern among Black voters about what data centers could mean for electricity costs.
Even with that protection described, 52 percent of Black voters expected data centers to raise electricity costs for everyday Americans.

title: Solar-powered 'leaf' generates hydrogen while purifying seawater
summary:
Inspired by leaves, which harness solar power to generate oxygen and carry out other processes, researchers at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore have developed a solar-powered device that generates hydrogen from seawater while simultaneously degrading hydrazine, a highly toxic industrial wastewater pollutant.
In conventional water electrolysis, hydrogen is produced at the cathode (negative electrode), while oxygen is released at the anode (positive electrode).
At the cathode, water molecules gain electrons and produce hydrogen gas, while at the anode, they lose electrons to produce oxygen.
As an alternative, the researchers developed an anode that, instead of producing oxygen, breaks down hydrazine, a highly toxic industrial pollutant.
So, is the device about to “revolutionize” global hydrogen production from seawater electrolysis?

title: Lufthansa Loses Greenwashing Lawsuit, Rebrands Green Fares As Impact Fares
summary:
Well, Lufthansa has now announced that it’s rebranding these fares, and the change isn’t voluntary…Lufthansa Green Fares become Impact FaresLufthansa Group is renaming its Green Fares, and going forward, they’ll be known as Impact Fares.
Here’s how Lufthansa describes this change:The Lufthansa Group is renaming its Green Fare to Impact Fare.
In March 2025, NGO Environmental Action Germany won a greenwashing lawsuit against Lufthansa related to these fares, on grounds of misleading consumers with sustainability claims.
These fares are now known as Impact Fares, with all the same perks as the previous Green Fares.

title: 40 years later, Chernobyl's nuclear fallout is not what scientists expected
summary:
Four decades after the Chernobyl (known today as Chornobyl) nuclear disaster, microscopic radioactive particles remain scattered throughout the surrounding soil.
However, the researchers emphasize that their findings should not be interpreted as evidence that Chornobyl's radioactive contamination is becoming harmless.
The relatively small sample means the findings cannot yet establish how radioactive particles behave throughout the entire contaminated region.
Why Chornobyl's Radioactive Legacy Remains UnpredictableEven with substantially more data, predicting the long term dangers of Chornobyl's radioactive debris would remain challenging.
Their work could provide a clearer picture of how Chornobyl's nuclear materials change over time and how long their environmental effects may persist.

title: The planet’s vital signs are getting worse. One of the easiest fixes is your diet.
summary:
Concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide, stemming primarily from the burning of fossil fuels, hit record highs this year.
Changes within our food system in particular present some of the easiest opportunities for individuals to help reduce greenhouse gas emissions, especially methane.
These two figures reflect “important pressures from the global food system,” said William Ripple, professor of ecology at Oregon State University and one of the report’s lead authors.
“At a time when climate change is threatening food security, we can hardly afford a food system that uses so much of its productive capacity inefficiently,” said Ripple.
“Our growing demand for meat is putting enormous pressure on the climate, land, and water at a time when all three are already under stress,” he said.

title: Singapore launches S$143 million initiative to help industries cut emissions
summary:
SINGAPORE: Singapore is launching a S$143 million (US$112 million) initiative to develop technologies that can help its industries reduce carbon emissions while remaining competitive.
It is compatible with Singapore's existing gas infrastructure, making it a potential option for industries seeking to lower their emissions.
"The sandbox will help pave the way for wider biomethane adoption, supporting up to 300 megawatts of capacity from 2028," said Mr Gan.
Speaking at the inaugural Singapore Industry Decarbonisation Forum, Mr Gan said helping industries go green was essential to Singapore's climate goals.
